top.title: An unexpected link: More coarse particles in indoor air, lower odds of Kawasaki disease
top.summary: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute inflammatory condition that primarily affects children under 5. It causes inflammation of blood vessels throughout the body and can lead to serious complications, particularly affecting the coronary arteries that supply blood to the heart. Although Kawasaki disease is a major cause of acquired heart disease in children, its exact cause remains unclear. Genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures are thought to contribute to its development, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood.

top.title: Wildfire smoke damages the airway's defenses, blocking one signal can shield them
top.summary: When the Palisades and Eaton wildfires tore through Los Angeles in January 2025, smoke blanketed the region and air quality plunged into the hazardous range. It was a vivid example of a growing problem: After years of improvement, wildfire smoke is pulling air quality back in the wrong direction, and fire season, once confined to hot, dry summers, now stretches across the year.

top.title: Alcohol, drug abuse, suicide: Is Europe really safe from America's 'deaths of despair' epidemic?
top.summary: In the United States, life expectancy diverged from Europe before it stopped rising during the 2010s, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. The economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton gave a name to a phenomenon that was then booming, partly explaining this trend: "deaths of despair," which have soared since the turn of the 21st century, especially among middle-aged white people without a college degree.

top.title: For military veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder, MDMA-assisted therapy may be safe, effective
top.summary: The first study of a program that uses the drug MDMA to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) plus alcohol use disorder in military veterans has concluded with promising results.

top.title: Brain clock gene influences alcohol consumption differently in female and male mice, study shows
top.summary: A gene that helps regulate the body's internal clock may influence alcohol consumption differently in males and females, according to new Concordia research.

top.title: Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12
top.summary: Scientists have found a surprising new use for vitamin B12, developing a rechargeable battery that uses the essential nutrient to help generate and store electricity. The prototype survived up to 250 charging cycles and could open the door to safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly alternatives to lithium-ion batteries.
top.text: Scientists have found an unexpected new use for vitamin B12, a nutrient best known for its importance to human health. Researchers at the University of Córdoba have incorporated the vitamin into a rechargeable battery, demonstrating for the first time that it can serve as a catalyst in this type of energy storage system. Vitamin B12 is essential for normal bodily function and is naturally present in animal products. The vitamin is produced by certain bacteria, which occur in nature and are also grown commercially to supply the food and pharmaceutical industries. In addition to its established applications in medicine, nutrition, and veterinary care, B12 is used to address certain nutritional deficiencies. It has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because of its potential to help reduce fatigue. Now, scientists are exploring an entirely different application. By using the vitamin to support the chemical reactions inside a battery, they have developed a prototype capable of completing up to 250 charging and discharging cycles. The new battery was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba's Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). It uses zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air to produce electricity, with vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, playing a crucial role in the process. To make the design work, the researchers attached vitamin B12 molecules to single-walled carbon nanotubes. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its center, which helps drive the electrochemical reactions needed for the battery to function. The team has previously experimented with natural molecules as battery catalysts, including hemoglobin and catalase. These substances contain iron (II) and iron (III), respectively. Vitamin B12 represents the group's third effort to use a biological molecule for this purpose, but it has delivered an important advance: a battery that can be recharged repeatedly, completing as many as 250 cycles. One of the biggest obstacles was keeping vitamin B12 inside the battery. Because the vitamin dissolves readily in water, it would normally be difficult to retain in a system that relies on a water-based electrolyte. The researchers overcame this problem by securing the vitamin to carbon nanotubes, using an approach inspired by how amino acids connect to form proteins. Manuel Cano Luna, one of the study's authors, explained that "we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries," while describing the team's search for useful biological compounds. Their attachment technique imitates "the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins." Alongside Cano Luna, the research team included Valentín García Caballero, Miguel López León, Pablo Gómez Argudo, Luis Camacho Delgado, José Miguel Rodríguez Mellado, María Teresa Martín Romero, José Abad López, and Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero. The findings, published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A , could contribute to the development of battery technologies that depend less on the materials used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. Although lithium-ion batteries are widely used, obtaining their raw materials can involve significant economic, environmental, and social challenges. Zinc-air batteries offer a potential alternative because they can store substantial amounts of energy relative to their weight while relying on materials that are more readily available. Zinc is abundant and recyclable, and these batteries use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as part of their energy-producing reactions. Because they draw oxygen from the air rather than storing all the necessary reactants internally, they can also be lighter than other battery designs. This advantage has helped make zinc-air batteries increasingly useful in compact electronic devices, particularly hearing aids. Another benefit is their use of non-flammable, water-based electrolytes, which can reduce fire risks and improve safety. A major challenge in developing rechargeable zinc-air batteries is finding a catalyst that can efficiently support the chemical reactions involved in both producing and storing electricity. During discharge, the battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Recharging requires the relevant chemical reactions to proceed in the opposite direction. A suitable catalyst must therefore be effective in both processes. According to researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero, vitamin B12 "has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen." This ability to support both reactions is what makes the vitamin particularly promising for rechargeable zinc-air battery technology. The successful prototype offers a new direction for researchers seeking affordable, sustainable alternatives to existing energy storage technologies. If the approach can be developed further, batteries using vitamin B12 catalysts could eventually help address one of the biggest challenges facing renewable energy: storing excess electricity generated by sources such as solar and wind power for use when production falls. Although the technology remains at the research stage, demonstrating up to 250 charge and discharge cycles shows that a familiar biological molecule can play an unexpected role in rechargeable battery design. The discovery adds to growing efforts to use naturally occurring substances to create safer, lighter, and more sustainable ways to store energy. Materials provided by University of Córdoba . top.title: Two measures to help prevent obesity in young people
top.summary: Obesity in children and young people increases the risk of health problems later in life to such an extent that tackling it is important, both for individuals and for the population as a whole. The condition is generally linked to diet and lifestyle. A new study including almost 125,000 children examines how best to help parents and children make healthier choices. The paper is published in the journal Acta Paediatrica.

top.title: When's a new organ not really new? Two anatomists explain
top.summary: People have been dissecting the human body for more than 2,500 years. In recent times, we've been over every nanometer with high-resolution medical imaging. So you'd think we know all there is to know about human anatomy. Surely, there are no new organs left to discover.

top.title: The child development 'sweet spot' that affects adult taste preference
top.summary: A baby's transition from breast milk or formula to a range of solid foods is the likely "sweet spot" for introducing nutritional variety that influences lifelong taste preferences by rewiring circuits in the brain, new research in mice suggests.

top.title: Adolescent and teen depression linked to heavier substance use
top.summary: Adolescents and teenagers who drink more alcohol or use multiple forms of marijuana are much more likely to experience major depression. In addition, girls, older teens and multiracial teens are more likely to experience major depression, regardless of drug or alcohol use.

top.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
top.summary: Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

top.title: New liver model for studying alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
top.summary: AATD is a rare genetic metabolic disorder that affects the liver and lungs. A mutation causes liver cells (hepatocytes) to form misfolded alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT). This misfolding results in reduced secretion of AAT into the blood plasma. AAT plays an important role in controlling inflammatory processes in the body by mitigating excessive reactions that lead to tissue damage.

top.title: A protein in the brain's immune cells may accelerate damage in Alzheimer's disease
top.summary: Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have identified a key role for the protein galectin-3 in Alzheimer's disease. The study shows that galectin-3 not only influences how the brain's immune cells, known as microglia, react to the disease's characteristic amyloid plaques but also shapes the plaques themselves—and may contribute to the nerve damage that develops around them.

top.title: Some people claim to speak many languages. But what does it really mean to be a polyglot?
top.summary: Roughly half of the world's population speaks more than one language. But speaking two or three languages is very different from claiming proficiency in five, 10 or more.

top.title: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides
top.summary: Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They're entirely undeterred by the radiation—in fact, some fungi even grow toward it.

top.title: California raised minimum wages for fast‑food workers—here's how it played out 2 years later
top.summary: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers' purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.

top.title: Deadly virus reduces tree frog population by 83% in Atlantic Forest reserve
top.summary: A highly lethal pathogen is responsible for the mass death of tadpoles and the rapid decline of amphibian populations in the Atlantic Forest. A group of researchers demonstrate for the first time in South America that recurring ranavirus outbreaks caused an 83% drop in monkey frog (Phyllomedusa distincta) reproduction in a pond in the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina. The disease is caused by a virus that affects reptiles and fish as well.

top.title: Capping nanovials that trap cells and their secretions for analysis enables new bioscience experiments
top.summary: A UCLA-developed technology that is like a test tube but on the cellular scale has led to a number of biomedical discoveries in recent years, including revelations about cancer, heart disease and the genetic levers that push cells to release proteins.

top.title: Whom do we expect to put others ahead of themselves: Boys or girls? New study has surprising, and unsurprising, answers
top.summary: The holiday season is a time for gatherings with family and friends—as well as for less festive but necessary duties: organizing, preparing for and cleaning up after these gatherings. These are examples of service tasks that, according to previous research, women and girls are expected to perform.

top.title: Cooking Thanksgiving dinner could create an indoor air quality problem inside your home, expert says
top.summary: The Thanksgiving turkey may be the centerpiece of the holiday meal, but cooking it, along with all the sides and other dishes, can invite an unexpected guest: indoor air pollution.

top.title: Tiny parasite holds big clues to help protect threatened estuarine turtles
top.summary: The diamondback terrapin is North America's only turtle species that lives exclusively in brackish coastal waters, such as salt marshes and estuaries. Its populations face threats from historical overharvesting and contemporary habitat loss, coastal development and accidental capture in crab traps.

top.title: How restaurants can make sustainable dining choices easier while still making a profit
top.summary: Canadians are eating out less. A 2025 survey found 57% of them are cooking at home more often to save money, while 69% of restaurant operators say customers are dining out less because of affordability. According to Restaurants Canada, 41% of operators are either losing money or breaking even.

top.title: How do human lifestyles affect the gut microbiome of our canine companions?
top.summary: Dogs have been living side by side with humans for millennia, but a new study underscores how much we have yet to learn about man's best friend. The study, which looked at hundreds of dogs across four nations, found that the lifestyles of pet owners appear to play a significant role in determining what constitutes a healthy gut microbiome for their dog companions.

top.title: Strange radio signals from space could come from a dead star
top.summary: The night sky is as good a place as any for a mystery. Back in 2002, astronomer Scott Hyman and his colleagues detected five mysterious bursts of radio waves coming from near the center of our galaxy, spaced roughly 77 minutes apart. The signals were detected again in 2003 and 2004, but then disappeared. Despite years of searching, there was no sign of their return.

top.title: Stem cell–derived nanoparticles modulate immune cells and help delay type 1 diabetes in mice
top.summary: In people with type 1 diabetes, the immune system mistakenly identifies insulin-producing cells in the pancreas as foreign and attacks them, leaving the body unable to properly regulate blood sugar. While insulin therapy helps manage the disease, it does not stop the underlying immune attack.

top.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
top.summary: About 1 in 4 US adults are family caregivers.
top.text: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people . The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion . Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 . But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.
facts: In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.
My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time.
That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.
The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid.
That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion .
The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care.
Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 .
Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving.
Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

top.title: Forms, phone calls and portals: The hidden work that keeps American institutions functioning burdens parents most
top.summary: Insurers, schools, doctors, benefits agencies – each has its own rules, databases, deadlines and definitions. Subtle misalignments compound over time, and the hassle falls heaviest on some groups.
top.text: As a working mom of three kids, I spend a lot of time parenting. I also spend a lot of time coordinating insurance, physician and school forms and remembering passwords to six different school and sports portals. None of that is really parenting, and it’s not paid work either, but it takes time away from both. I’m also a political theorist who studies how institutional design affects people’s daily lives. What many people characterize as unavoidable aspects of modern life actually provide important lessons about how various institutions are set up and who does the work to keep them functional. Most American families deal with multiple complex institutions every week: a personalized mix of health insurers and medical providers, schools, tax authorities, Social Security and benefits agencies, daycares and camps and other kid activities, and state and federal programs such as Medicaid or SNAP. Each of these programs has its own logic, including specific rules, portals, databases, forms, deadlines and definitions. This variation creates subtle misalignments across programs that compound over time. The physician needs prior authorization from the insurer, but the insurer claims the doctor needs a specific form. Meanwhile, the school needs the doctor’s document, and a benefits office might need proof that another agency already has in its system. The people working to align all these systems are parents , often people with the least time and cognitive availability to handle the burden. Political scientists Pamela Herd and Donald Moynihan of the Better Government Lab call this load administrative burden ; that burden includes learning all the rules, figuring out how to comply with them, and then handling all the rippling demands that each individual task creates. These burdens are not natural or inevitable. Instead, they’re the result of the way people have designed our institutions. The good news is that it’s possible to do things differently. Most institutions weren’t intentionally designed with the user experience in mind. Instead, they’re the result of piecemeal decisions over decades, often the result of a complex interplay of interest-group lobbying, political jockeying and public demands. Employer-based health insurance resulted, in part, from fear of socialized medicine during World War II. Public schools grew out of local communities and then had layers of state and federal regulations piled on top. Bureaucracies at different levels and of different types rarely talk to each other or bother coordinating their rules and processes. And most of these rules and processes aren’t usually nefarious in intent . Documentation can prevent fraud, eligibility rules help allocate scarce resources, regulations can protect patients, and institutions have a vested interest in protecting themselves from mistakes and liability. But each operates in isolation. The cracks are visible only to the person who has to navigate these silos – and that’s often an overextended parent. It might seem like everyone bears the same administrative burdens, but they don’t. Life administration hits some groups harder than others; women , people with disabilities and lower-income people all interact more frequently with these fragmented systems and are less able to absorb the costs of those interactions. For a middle-class American on salary, an hour on hold is a nuisance. For a waitress working for tips, it’s lost earnings or even lost employment. For many Americans, the administrative burden of applying for and proving eligibility for benefits is dramatic; the people who need these programs the most struggle to access them . This is what researchers call a regressive effect in public policy, meaning that the costs hit hardest for those who can least afford it. Many institutions are effectively means-tested in reverse: The most vulnerable pay the most in terms of time, energy and money. While there is no easy fix with institutions as complex as healthcare, education or public benefits, there are some options. One useful model is universal design : the idea that we should build our environments – in this case, institutions – for people of different abilities from the start. On the institutional front, this would mean more flexible hours to accommodate a range of users; a combination of email, phone and platform access; automatic enrollment or renewal when eligibility is already known; various plain language rules; and agencies sharing information, with permission, and working together to resolve conflicts between policies and rules so families aren’t forced into the role of unpaid institutional coordinators. Much of this will require not just language rewrites but significant investment in new systems . Michigan provides an example of reform working at scale. In 2018 the state consolidated benefit application forms across five programs, reducing length and complexity. The original combined application packet was an overwhelming 1,000 questions and over 64 pages long. The streamlined application process, which could be completed in about 20 minutes, not only improved the process for those applying. It reduced errors, cut down worker processing time and saved caseworkers 200,000 hours per year, presumably saving tax dollars along the way. Reducing administrative burden across programs is one of the few policy reforms with almost no downside. For now, many Americans are like fish swimming in polluted water. We know something’s wrong, but we can’t see the cause. The next time you’re stuck on hold trying to fix a paperwork error with one agency before you can submit additional paperwork to another, it’s worthwhile to remember that this experience isn’t an inevitability of modern life. It’s the result of design choices – or failure to make choices – that can be changed.

top.title: Florida’s flooding déjà vu is a sign of things to come – so, who is most at risk and how can they prepare?
top.summary: More than a foot of rain flooded streets in the already saturated region in mid-November 2026, with more forecast in the days ahead.
top.text: Floodwater filled the streets and crept into homes across Florida’s Atlantic coast as an intense storm dumped more than a foot of rain in 24 hours starting Nov. 17, 2026. The deluge followed extreme downpours in parts of the region less than three weeks earlier , and forecasters warned of more rain still to come . As people in Fort Lauderdale watched the water rise in their already saturated yards, it may have felt like déjà vu. In April 2023, more than 25 inches of rain fell in Fort Lauderdale in 24 hours. Even hurricanes rarely drop that much rain in one area that fast. Residents could do little to stop the flooding. Studies show that as global temperatures rise, more people will be at risk from such destructive flooding – including in areas that rarely faced extreme flooding in the past. In many of these communities, the people at greatest risk of harm from flash flooding are low-wage workers , older adults and other vulnerable residents who live in low-lying areas and who have few resources to protect their properties and themselves. I study the impact of extreme weather on vulnerable communities as an associate professor of social work . To limit the damage, communities need to know who is at risk and how they can be better prepared. The Florida storms offer a view into the risks ahead as temperatures rise . These risks are especially high as the effects of a strong 2026-27 El Niño set in . A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture , leading to stronger downpours. The resulting deluges can be devastating. These events are expected to increase in frequency and intensity in many regions as greenhouse gas emissions from human activities continue to heat up the planet . Recent disasters show how the risk of flash flooding is expanding beyond areas traditionally considered at risk . To plan for extreme weather, it’s crucial for community leaders and residents to know where the risks are highest and who might not be prepared . Low-lying areas with poorly planned development , lack of investment in protective infrastructure and the lingering effects of historic disinvestment and discrimination are often at higher risk. So are low-income communities with tight budgets that can’t afford protective measures like upgraded levees or stormwater systems and can’t recover from damage quickly. When older adults live in these flood-prone areas , they are at even higher risk. Older adults have a higher likelihood of having health needs or some form of disability that could affect their ability to leave quickly during a disaster. They are also more likely to be socially isolated , which may mean they don’t hear timely information or have help to evacuate or quick access to resources for recovering. My colleagues and I have examined how prepared people are for disasters of any kind across the U.S. – flooding, tornadoes, hurricanes and others – and how housing security played a role. The numbers are sobering. Overall, we found in a 2023 study that 57% of the population, among 29,070 housing units surveyed nationwide, reported they were not prepared with food, water, emergency funds and transportation in case disaster struck. We found that households facing housing insecurity – those behind on their payments for rent, mortgage or utilities – were less prepared for disasters than others, even when the occupants had similar incomes and education. People who are struggling to meet day-to-day needs often don’t have the ability and resources to plan for everyday events, let alone for disasters. Our research has shown that households with children, households led by women, and low-income households were less prepared than others for disasters. Renting adds additional challenges. In the U.S., lower-income families often depend on the rental market . They tend to move more frequently, and since they don’t own the property, they often can’t make upgrades for safety. And landlords might not prioritize those risks that seem rare but carry costs. The most effective way to address these challenges is through solutions that are tailored to the community. That can involve investing in infrastructure , including state-funded priorities such as drainage systems, large-scale flood prevention measures and strengthening the power grid , as well as ensuring that people have access to safe and affordable housing . Some communities and federal agencies have bought out properties that frequently flood and changed zoning rules to prevent more people from moving into harm’s way. Raising community awareness about climate change and extreme weather risks is also crucial, especially among those most at risk , such as older adults and other socially marginalized groups . If people understand the risks, know how to prepare their homes, know how to plan for emergencies , know whom to contact for help, and have stronger systems of care, they’re more likely to be prepared when disasters strike. I believe the most successful efforts are those that bring at-risk communities into planning discussions . For example, in Columbus, Ohio, the city partnered with the Central Ohio Area Agency on Aging, Age Friendly Innovation Center and my team to improve disaster preparedness among older residents . We worked with older adults in affordable housing communities and the human service professionals who support them to help design action plans for communities with special needs in the event of an emergency. The tool kit we created can help social service providers prepare low-income residents for extreme weather. Our team is now working with service providers nationwide to document best practices, identify gaps and ensure residents are better prepared for climate- and weather-related emergencies in the future. top.title: How to protect your retirement savings if the AI boom fizzles
top.summary: Many savers don’t know how much of their 401(k) funds are weighted toward Big Tech companies.
top.text: After stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south. While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks . Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year. As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing. Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it. Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund , which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s important to first explain how these funds work. About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you. Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund . About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion . Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices : U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds. For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund , who expect to retire imminently. That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia. In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers , Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4% . Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned . By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month. That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar. More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement plan on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility. Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit. But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold . And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies. By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500 , according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings. In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly. Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund , with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a big impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix. And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips. Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average . In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing. But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund. For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone . The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest. First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year. Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk. Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests. About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly . For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do. Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund , and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times. Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target. Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each. None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. Bu
